messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

At 46, Minh Tran had spent years in American firehouses learning how to move toward danger, and that identity had once given him a clear place in the world. Before that, he had worked as a relief worker in a war zone, attached to teams pulling civilians from damaged buildings after shelling. The event he returns to most often is not one clean scene but a shattered sequence around an explosion at a crowded shelter. He remembers a sudden bang, the pressure in his body, pain striking through his side and legs, dust, shouting, and then fragments he cannot reliably place in order: a child crying, a doorway blocked, a woman begging, men pushing past others to get out first, someone making a crude remark about what had happened to women in another district. When he tries to tell it, the words fail him at the worst points. He says he knows what happened, but “it won’t line up,” and often stops speaking altogether, rubbing at the places in his body that hurt again when the memory comes.

In the years since, specific moments in ordinary life pull those fragments back with unnerving force. At the station, if equipment drops with a sharp bang or a call comes in over radio chatter followed by a sudden blast from a training video, he is no longer just in the apparatus bay; the scene returns in broken pieces, and with it the same bodily pain. Comments about sexual violence, even overheard casually in the locker room or in news coverage playing in the kitchen, bring back the shelter and what he believes he failed to stop. People misbehaving in small selfish ways—drivers ignoring emergency lanes, bystanders filming instead of helping, younger firefighters laughing off suffering—hit him harder than he can explain. In those moments he is flooded not only with the memory but with the conviction that he crossed lines he can never uncross, that under pressure he acted against the man he believed himself to be.

What has taken hold most deeply is the meaning Minh gives those memories. He has come to believe his life was destroyed there, not in the dramatic sense of physical ruin but in the quieter sense that nothing since has fit. Divorced and increasingly detached at the station, he feels he belongs nowhere: not with civilians who have not seen what he saw, not with the men he served beside overseas, and not fully with his firefighting crew, who know him as competent but distant. The more the memory breaks apart when he tries to recount it, the more certain he becomes that this confusion reflects something rotten in him—that he did something unforgivable and cannot even speak it plainly. Those conclusions make his triggers feel even more charged. A bang is not only a sound; it is proof that the past is waiting. Silence is not rest; in a room gone suddenly quiet, he becomes certain danger is about to break through.

From there, his days have narrowed around managing what feels unmanageable. He tries hard not to think about the war zone at all, cutting off conversations, changing channels, forcing his mind blank during the commute. He performs private mental rituals—repeating phrases, counting in set patterns, silently reviewing who is on shift—in the belief that if he does them correctly, something terrible may be prevented. When the pressure rises too high, especially after a vivid return of the shelter or an evening spent stewing over what kind of man he was there, he has hurt himself physically to release the surge inside. He describes this without drama, as if it were grim maintenance.

Yet these efforts have tightened the problem around him. The harder Minh suppresses the memories, the more they return jagged and unsorted, with the same bodily pain and speechless panic. The rituals briefly steady him, but they also keep him scanning for signs he has missed something, so that unusual silence on a call, an offhand cruel joke, or a distant bang can ignite fear, anger, guilt, and shame all at once. His irritability has become harder to contain. At work he snaps at probies for minor mistakes and has shoved a locker door so hard a captain pulled him aside. Afterward he sees this anger as further evidence that he is no longer who he was, which only deepens his sense that he has been ruined.

What finally brought Minh to treatment was an incident at the firehouse kitchen. A television segment mentioned sexual violence in a conflict zone, someone muttered a crude comment, and in the silence that followed he felt the old danger gather in the room. His chest and legs flared with pain; the memory came back in disordered flashes; then he erupted at a coworker with a ferocity that frightened everyone, including himself. Later, alone, he was overwhelmed by the thought that he could not keep living divided between numbness and sudden violence. He is seeking help because he is afraid that if this continues he will lose the only work he still knows how to do, and because some part of him still hopes it might be possible to speak what happened without being destroyed by it.
